solution:
A paint or a lubricating oil is useful only if it **spreads out into a thin, even film that wets the whole surface**, instead of gathering itself into separate drops.
Whether a liquid spreads is decided by its angle of contact. For a drop resting on a solid the chapter's equilibrium condition is
\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_3}\)
where \(T_3\) is the surface tension of the liquid itself. Making \(T_3\) small makes the right-hand side large: the angle of contact becomes small, and once \((T_2 - T_1) > T_3\) the equation would require \(\cos\theta > 1\), which is impossible — the chapter's own conclusion for that case is that "the liquid spreads over the solid surface and drop will not be formed".
So a low surface tension gives
- a small angle of contact and good wetting,
- easy spreading into a thin uniform coat (paint), and
- the ability to creep into the narrow gaps between moving parts (lubricating oil).
A high-surface-tension liquid would instead bead up, leaving the surface patchy and the bearing surfaces dry.

A **soap bubble has two free surfaces** in contact with air — an inner one and an outer one — so its total surface area is twice that of a sphere of the same radius.
Starting from zero radius, the increase in surface area is
\(dA = 2 \times 4\pi r^2 = 8\pi r^2\)
The work done is stored as surface energy, so
\(W = T \, dA = 8\pi r^2 T\)
where \(T\) is the surface tension of the soap solution.
Note the factor of 2: for a **liquid drop**, which has only one surface, the same calculation gives \(W = 4\pi r^2 T\).

Bernoulli's principle rests on the **work-energy theorem**, and hence on the **conservation of energy**.
In the chapter's derivation the net work done on a fluid element by the pressure of the surrounding fluid is equated to the sum of the changes in its kinetic and potential energies:
\((P_1 - P_2)\,dV = \Delta K.E. + \Delta P.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho\,dV\left(v_2^2 - v_1^2\right) + \rho\,dV g(h_2 - h_1)\)
which rearranges to \(P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \) constant. Every term has the dimensions of energy per unit volume, so the equation says that the total energy per unit volume of the fluid is the same at every point along a streamline. As the chapter puts it, "Bernoulli's principle is thus consistent with the principle of conservation of energy."
It holds only for a **steady, streamline, incompressible and non-viscous** flow — viscosity would dissipate energy and the constant would not be constant.

A manometer reads a pressure difference as a **difference of liquid levels**, through
\(p - p_0 = h\rho g \qquad \therefore h = \dfrac{p - p_0}{\rho g}\)
For a given pressure difference the level difference \(h\) is **inversely proportional to the density** \(\rho\) of the manometric liquid. A low-density liquid such as water or kerosene therefore gives a much larger \(h\) than mercury would, and a large \(h\) can be read off the scale more easily and with a smaller percentage error — that is, the instrument is more sensitive. The chapter says exactly this: the U-tube is "partly filled with a low density liquid such as water or kerosene. This helps in having a larger level difference between the level of liquid in the two arms."
There is a second, practical reason the chapter gives elsewhere: mercury vapours are hazardous, so mercury is not advised in a school laboratory.

An **incompressible fluid** is one whose **density does not change when pressure is applied** — a given mass of it keeps the same volume however hard it is squeezed, so \(\rho\) is constant throughout the flow.
No real fluid is perfectly incompressible, but liquids change their volume so little under ordinary pressures that they are treated as incompressible; gases are not.
The assumption is what makes the equation of continuity take its simple form: with \(\rho\) the same at both sections, \(\rho A_1 v_1 = \rho A_2 v_2\) reduces to \(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\), i.e. \(Av = \) constant.

Because merging **reduces the total surface area**, and hence the surface energy, of the mercury.
Surface energy \(= T \times\) (surface area). Suppose \(n\) equal drops of radius \(r\) merge into one drop of radius \(R\). Volume is conserved, so
\(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \qquad \therefore R = n^{1/3} r\)
Area before \(= n \times 4\pi r^2\); area after \(= 4\pi R^2 = n^{2/3} \times 4\pi r^2\).
Since \(n^{2/3} < n\) for every \(n > 1\), the final area is **smaller** than the initial area, so the surface energy decreases and the excess energy is released to the surroundings.
As the chapter states, any system tends to a state of minimum potential energy, so a liquid always tries to minimise its surface area. Mercury has very strong cohesive forces and does not wet glass, so nothing holds the separate drops apart and they run together into one drop the moment they touch.

Because of the **equation of continuity**, which is just conservation of mass for the flowing water.
Water is incompressible and cannot leave through the walls of the pipe, so whatever volume enters the broad section per second must leave the narrow section per second:
\(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \qquad \therefore v \propto \dfrac{1}{A}\)
The narrow pipe offers a smaller cross-sectional area, so the same volume per second can only get through if it moves faster. In the chapter's words, "because the fluid is incompressible, the particles move faster through a narrow section and slow down while moving through a wider section" — if it did not speed up, the water would have to be compressed to fit into the smaller space, which it cannot be.

The two effects have two different causes, and they must be given separately.
**The speed increases** because of the equation of continuity: \(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\), so the smaller area at the constriction forces a larger speed (the same volume per second must pass through).
**The pressure falls** because of Bernoulli's equation. The pipe is horizontal, so \(h_1 = h_2\) and the potential-energy term drops out, leaving
\(P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2\)
i.e. \(P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 = \) constant. If \(v_2 > v_1\) then \(P_2 < P_1\): where the speed is greater the pressure is smaller.
Physically, the liquid entering the constriction is being **accelerated**, and the only forward force available is the pressure of the fluid behind it, so the pressure behind must exceed the pressure ahead. The total energy per unit volume is unchanged — kinetic energy is simply gained at the expense of pressure energy.

Consider a spherical drop of radius \(r\), with pressure \(p_{\text{i}}\) inside and \(p_{\text{o}}\) outside. Because the surface is curved the inside pressure is the greater, and \(p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}}\) is the excess pressure to be found.
Let the radius increase by a very small amount \(\Delta r\), so small that the pressure inside stays practically constant.
Initial surface area \(A_1 = 4\pi r^2\)
Final surface area \(A_2 = 4\pi (r + \Delta r)^2 = 4\pi\left(r^2 + 2r\Delta r + \Delta r^2\right)\)
As \(\Delta r\) is very small, \(\Delta r^2\) is negligible, so \(A_2 = 4\pi r^2 + 8\pi r \Delta r\).
Increase in surface area:
\(dA = A_2 - A_1 = 8\pi r \Delta r\)
The work done in creating this extra area is stored as surface energy:
\(dW = T\,dA = T\,(8\pi r \Delta r) \qquad \ldots (1)\)
The same work is done by the excess pressure pushing the surface out through \(\Delta r\). The outward force is (excess pressure) \(\times\) (surface area):
\(F = (p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}})\,4\pi r^2\)
\(\therefore dW = F\,\Delta r = (p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}})\,4\pi r^2 \Delta r \qquad \ldots (2)\)
Equating (1) and (2),
\(T\,(8\pi r \Delta r) = (p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}})\,4\pi r^2 \Delta r\)
\(\therefore p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}} = \dfrac{2T}{r}\)
This is the excess pressure inside a liquid drop; it is called **Laplace's law of a spherical membrane**.
**Note the factor of 2 that separates a drop from a bubble.** A drop has ONE liquid-air surface. A **soap bubble** has two, so its increase in area is \(dA = 2(8\pi r \Delta r)\) and the same argument gives \(p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}} = \dfrac{4T}{r}\).

Consider a tube of flow in the steady flow of a fluid, and two cross sections of it — \(A_1\) at a point A and \(A_2\) at a point B. All the fluid that passes through the tube of flow must cross every such section; fluid can neither enter nor leave through the walls of the tube.
Let the speed at A be \(v_1\). In a time interval \(\Delta t\) the fluid at A advances a distance \(v_1 \Delta t\), so the mass entering through A is
\(m_1 = \rho A_1 v_1 \Delta t\)
Similarly, with speed \(v_2\) at B, the mass leaving through B in the same interval is
\(m_2 = \rho A_2 v_2 \Delta t\)
Matter is neither created nor destroyed within the region between the two sections, and for a steady flow the mass held in that region does not change with time. Therefore the mass entering must equal the mass leaving:
\(\rho A_1 v_1 \Delta t = \rho A_2 v_2 \Delta t\)
This is the statement of **conservation of mass**. Cancelling \(\Delta t\) gives the general (mass-flux) form
\(\rho A_1 v_1 = \rho A_2 v_2\), i.e. \(\rho A v = \dfrac{dm}{dt} = \) constant
and for an **incompressible** fluid \(\rho\) is the same at both sections and cancels, leaving
\(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\) or \(Av = \) constant
So the equation of continuity is nothing but conservation of mass written for a fluid in steady flow: the quantity \(Av\) is the volume flux \(dV/dt\) and \(\rho A v\) is the mass flux \(dm/dt\), and it is the same through every cross section.

**Capillary action (capillarity)** is the rise or fall of a liquid inside a tube of very fine bore when the tube is dipped into the liquid.
Which of the two happens depends on whether the liquid wets the tube:
- a liquid that **wets** the tube (water in glass) has an acute angle of contact and a **concave** meniscus, and its level **rises**;
- a liquid that **does not wet** the tube (mercury in glass) has an obtuse angle of contact and a **convex** meniscus, and its level **falls**.
**Why it happens.** The pressure on the concave side of a curved liquid surface is always greater than that on the convex side, by \(\dfrac{2T}{R}\). Take four points as in the chapter: A just above the meniscus inside the tube, B just below it inside, C just above the flat liquid surface outside, D just below it outside, with B and D at the same horizontal level.
Outside the tube the surface is plane, so \(p_{\text{A}} = p_{\text{C}} = p_{\text{D}} = \) atmospheric pressure.
For **water**, the meniscus is concave upward, so the air side (A) is the concave side and \(p_{\text{B}} = p_{\text{A}} - \dfrac{2T}{R} < p_{\text{D}}\). Two points at the same level are at unequal pressures, so water flows into the capillary and rises. It stops rising when the weight of the raised column supplies the missing pressure, i.e. when \(h\rho g = \dfrac{2T}{R}\).
For **mercury**, the meniscus is convex, so \(p_{\text{B}} > p_{\text{D}}\) at the same level and mercury is pushed out of the capillary until the level has dropped enough to balance.
**Everyday examples**: oil rising up the wick of a lamp, a cloth rag sucking up water, water rising in the crevices of rocks, sap rising to the topmost leaves of a tree, and blotting paper absorbing ink.

Let a capillary tube of radius \(r\) be dipped in a liquid of density \(\rho\) and surface tension \(T\) which wets the tube, so that the meniscus is **concave** and the angle of contact \(\theta\) is acute. Let \(h\) be the height to which the liquid rises and \(R\) the radius of curvature of the meniscus.
**Method I — using the pressure difference.**
The pressure just below the concave meniscus is less than the atmospheric pressure just above it by \(\dfrac{2T}{R}\). This deficit must be made up by the pressure of the raised liquid column, so
\(h\rho g = \dfrac{2T}{R}\)
From the geometry of the meniscus (the tube radius \(r\) is the projection of \(R\)),
\(R = \dfrac{r}{\cos\theta}\)
\(\therefore h\rho g = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r}\)
\(\therefore h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\)
**Method II — using forces.**
The liquid is in contact with the tube along its circumference \(2\pi r\), so the force due to surface tension is
\(f_T = T \times 2\pi r\)
acting along the tangent to the meniscus, i.e. at the angle of contact \(\theta\) to the wall. Its vertical component is
\((f_T)_v = T \times 2\pi r \cos\theta\)
Ignoring the small amount of liquid in the meniscus itself, the volume of the raised column is \(\pi r^2 h\), so its weight is
\(w = \pi r^2 h \rho g\)
At equilibrium the weight is balanced by the vertical component of the force of surface tension:
\(\pi r^2 h \rho g = T \times 2\pi r \cos\theta\)
\(\therefore h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\)
the same result. Rearranged for the surface tension,
\(T = \dfrac{rh\rho g}{2\cos\theta}\)
**Two things worth noting.** Since \(\theta\) is acute for a concave meniscus, \(\cos\theta\) is positive and \(h\) is positive — a genuine rise. And \(h \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\): the narrower the tube the higher the liquid climbs. The same expression covers a convex meniscus, where \(\theta\) is obtuse, \(\cos\theta\) is negative and \(h\) comes out negative, i.e. a capillary fall.

**Given:** \(h = 200\) m, \(\rho = 1060\) kg/m\(^3\), \(p_0 = 1\) atm \(= 1.013 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
The pressure at a depth \(h\) below a free surface which is itself at pressure \(p_0\) is
\(p = p_0 + h\rho g\)
Pressure due to the sea water alone:
\(h\rho g = 200 \times 1060 \times 9.8 = 2.0776 \times 10^{6}\) N/m\(^2\)
Adding the atmospheric pressure on the free surface:
\(p = 1.013 \times 10^{5} + 2.0776 \times 10^{6}\)
\(p = 2.1789 \times 10^{6}\) N/m\(^2 = 21.789 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\)
This is the **absolute** pressure, about 21.5 times atmospheric. Had the question asked for the gauge pressure, the answer would have been the \(2.0776 \times 10^{6}\) N/m\(^2\) due to the water alone.

**Given:** \(A_1 = 30\) cm\(^2\), \(A_2 = 1500\) cm\(^2\), \(F_1 = 25\) N.
By **Pascal's law** the pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished, so the pressure is the same under both pistons:
\(\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}\)
\(\therefore F_2 = F_1 \times \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = 25 \times \dfrac{1500}{30} = 25 \times 50\)
\(F_2 = 1250\) N
The weight that can be supported on the output piston is **1250 N** (a mass of about 128 kg).
Note that only the *ratio* of the areas enters, so there is no need to convert cm\(^2\) to m\(^2\). The force is multiplied 50 times — but the output piston moves 50 times less far, so no energy is created.

**Given:** diameter \(= 1\) mm, so \(r = 0.5\) mm \(= 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m; \(v = 2\) m/s; \(\eta = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) N s/m\(^2\).
By **Stokes' law** the viscous force on a small sphere moving through a viscous medium is
\(F = 6\pi\eta r v\)
\(F = 6 \times 3.142 \times \left(1.8 \times 10^{-5}\right) \times \left(5 \times 10^{-4}\right) \times 2\)
\(F = 3.393 \times 10^{-7}\) N
The viscous force is **3.393 \(\times 10^{-7}\) N**, directed **upward** — opposite to the drop's motion. Since the drop is said to be falling with a *uniform* velocity, this is its terminal condition, and the viscous force together with the upthrust balances the weight.
The commonest slip here is to use the diameter in place of the radius; that would give twice this answer.

**Given:** \(F = 1\) N, \(A = 10^{-2}\) m\(^2\), \(v = 2 \times 10^{-2}\) m/s, thickness of the oil layer \(d = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\) m.
The plate moves with a constant velocity, so the applied force is exactly balanced by the viscous drag. The oil layer is thin, so the velocity gradient across it is uniform:
\(\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v}{d}\)
From Newton's law of viscosity,
\(F = \eta A \dfrac{v}{d} \qquad \therefore \eta = \dfrac{F d}{A v}\)
\(\eta = \dfrac{1 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{\left(10^{-2}\right) \times \left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(\eta = 7.5\) N s/m\(^2\)
The coefficient of viscosity of the oil is **7.5 N s/m\(^2\)** (that is, 7.5 Pa s, or 75 poise, since 1 Pa s = 10 poise).

**Given:** diameter \(= 0.4\) mm, so \(r = 0.2\) mm \(= 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m; \(\eta = 0.1\) N s/m\(^2\); specific gravity of the liquid \(= 0.9\), so \(\sigma = 0.9 \times 1000 = 900\) kg/m\(^3\); density of air \(\rho = 1.29\) kg/m\(^3\); \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
The terminal velocity of a sphere in a viscous medium is
\(v = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}\)
Here the sphere is a bubble of **air** and the medium is the **liquid**, so \(\rho = 1.29\) and \(\sigma = 900\). Substituting:
\(v = \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{\left(2 \times 10^{-4}\right)^2 \times (1.29 - 900) \times 9.8}{0.1}\)
\(v = \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{\left(4 \times 10^{-8}\right) \times (-898.71) \times 9.8}{0.1}\)
\(v = -7.83 \times 10^{-4}\) m/s
The **magnitude of the terminal velocity is \(7.83 \times 10^{-4}\) m/s** (about 0.78 mm/s), and the **negative sign means the bubble moves upward** — it rises, because the air inside it is far less dense than the liquid around it. The buoyant force exceeds the weight, and the bubble settles at the speed at which the viscous drag makes up the difference.

**Given:** \(d_1 = 10\) cm, \(v_1 = 2\) m/s, \(v_2 = 4\) m/s.
Water is incompressible, so by the equation of continuity
\(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\)
For a circular pipe \(A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}\), so the \(\pi/4\) cancels and
\(d_1^2 v_1 = d_2^2 v_2\)
\(\therefore d_2 = d_1 \sqrt{\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}} = 10 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{4}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\(d_2 = 7.07\) cm \(= 7.07 \times 10^{-2}\) m
The nozzle's internal diameter must be **\(7.07 \times 10^{-2}\) m**. Note that doubling the speed does not halve the diameter — it divides it by \(\sqrt{2}\), because the area, not the diameter, is what is inversely proportional to the speed.

**Given:** gauge pressure \(p = 4 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\), \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\).
Apply Bernoulli's equation between a point just inside the tank at the orifice and a point just outside it, both at the same level. Before the flow starts the water inside is at rest, and the water emerging is at atmospheric pressure, so the whole of the gauge pressure is converted into kinetic energy per unit volume:
\(p = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2\)
\(\therefore v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2p}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 4 \times 10^{5}}{1000}} = \sqrt{800}\)
\(v = 28.28\) m/s
The speed of efflux is **28.28 m/s**.
(This is Torricelli's result in another dress: writing the gauge pressure as \(p = h\rho g\) turns \(v = \sqrt{2p/\rho}\) into \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\).)

**Given:** \(P_1 = 3 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\) (valve closed), \(P_2 = 2 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^2\) (valve open), \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\).
While the valve is closed the water is **at rest**, so \(v_1 = 0\). When the valve is opened the water flows and the pressure drops to \(P_2\). The pipe is at one level, so the potential-energy term is the same at both stages and Bernoulli's equation gives
\(P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2\)
\(\therefore P_1 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2\)
\(\therefore v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times \left(3 \times 10^{5} - 2 \times 10^{5}\right)}{1000}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 10^{5}}{1000}} = \sqrt{200}\)
\(v = 14.14\) m/s
The water flows through the pipe at **14.14 m/s**. The pressure the water loses is exactly the pressure energy per unit volume that has been turned into kinetic energy.

**Given:** \(r = 0.1\) mm \(= 1 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(T = 7 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m, \(\theta = 0^\circ\) so \(\cos\theta = 1\), \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
The capillary rise is
\(h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\)
\(h = \dfrac{2 \times \left(7 \times 10^{-2}\right) \times 1}{\left(1 \times 10^{-4}\right) \times 1000 \times 9.8}\)
\(h = \dfrac{0.14}{0.98}\)
\(h = 0.1429\) m
The water rises through **0.1429 m**, that is about 14.3 cm.
The radius here is the radius of the **tube**, not its diameter — using 0.2 mm would halve the answer.

**Given:** \(r = 0.2\) mm \(= 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(T = 7.2 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m.
**Decide first how many surfaces there are — this is where the question is won or lost.** An air bubble sitting *inside* water is a cavity in the liquid, bounded by a **single** water-air interface. It is therefore governed by the drop formula
\(p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}} = \dfrac{2T}{r}\)
and **not** by the soap-bubble formula \(4T/r\), which applies only to a film with two free surfaces, such as a soap bubble blown in air.
The bubble is situated just below the water surface, so the depth is negligible and the term \(h\rho g\) can be dropped. The gauge pressure inside the bubble is then just the excess pressure:
\(p = \dfrac{2T}{r} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{0.144}{2 \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(p = 720\) N/m\(^2\)
The gauge pressure is **720 N/m\(^2\)**. (Using \(4T/r\) by mistake would have given 1440 N/m\(^2\) — exactly twice too large.)

**Given:** \(n = 27\), \(r = 0.1\) mm \(= 1 \times 10^{-4}\) m, \(T = 0.072\) N/m.
**Radius of the single drop.** Volume is conserved when the droplets coalesce:
\(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 27 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \qquad \therefore R = (27)^{1/3} r = 3r = 3 \times 10^{-4}\) m
**Areas.** A liquid drop has one surface, so
initial area \(= 27 \times 4\pi r^2 = 27 \times 4\pi \times \left(10^{-4}\right)^2 = 3.393 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
final area \(= 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi \times \left(3 \times 10^{-4}\right)^2 = 1.131 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
decrease in area \(= dA = 4\pi\left(27r^2 - R^2\right) = 4\pi\left(27 \times 10^{-8} - 9 \times 10^{-8}\right) = 2.262 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
**Change in surface energy.**
\(\Delta E = T \times dA = 0.072 \times 2.262 \times 10^{-6}\)
\(\Delta E = 1.628 \times 10^{-7}\) J \(= 1.628\) erg
The surface energy **decreases** by \(1.628 \times 10^{-7}\) J. Since the area gets smaller, no work has to be done on the drops — this energy is **released to the surroundings**, mostly as heat, which is why a coalescing spray warms very slightly.

**Given:** \(R = 0.2\) cm \(= 2 \times 10^{-3}\) m, \(n = 8\) droplets, \(T = 435.5\) dyne/cm.
**Convert the surface tension to SI.** \(1\) dyne \(= 10^{-5}\) N and \(1\) cm \(= 10^{-2}\) m, so \(1\) dyne/cm \(= 10^{-3}\) N/m.
\(T = 435.5 \times 10^{-3} = 0.4355\) N/m
**Radius of each droplet.** Volume is conserved:
\(8 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \qquad \therefore r = \dfrac{R}{(8)^{1/3}} = \dfrac{R}{2} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\) m
**Increase in area.** Mercury drops have one surface each:
\(dA = 8 \times 4\pi r^2 - 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi\left(8r^2 - R^2\right)\)
\(dA = 4\pi\left(8 \times 10^{-6} - 4 \times 10^{-6}\right) = 4\pi \times 4 \times 10^{-6} = 5.027 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^2\)
**Work done.**
\(W = T \times dA = 0.4355 \times 5.027 \times 10^{-5}\)
\(W = 2.189 \times 10^{-5}\) J
The work done is **\(2.189 \times 10^{-5}\) J**. Here the area **increases**, so unlike the coalescing case this work has to be **supplied to** the mercury from outside.

**Given:** \(R = 2\) cm \(= 0.02\) m, \(T = 0.07\) N/m.
A **soap bubble has two free surfaces** — an inner and an outer one — so the area created in blowing it from nothing is twice the area of a sphere:
\(dA = 2 \times 4\pi R^2 = 8\pi R^2\)
\(dA = 8 \times 3.142 \times (0.02)^2 = 8 \times 3.142 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 1.0053 \times 10^{-2}\) m\(^2\)
The work done is stored as surface energy:
\(W = T \times dA = 0.07 \times 1.0053 \times 10^{-2}\)
\(W = 7.037 \times 10^{-4}\) J \(= 0.7038 \times 10^{-3}\) J
The work required is **\(0.7038 \times 10^{-3}\) J**.
If this were a liquid **drop** of the same radius, with only one surface, the answer would be half as much, \(3.52 \times 10^{-4}\) J.

**Given:** the film grows from 2 cm \(\times\) 2 cm to 3 cm \(\times\) 3 cm; \(T = 3 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m.
A soap film stretched on a frame has **two surfaces**, a front one and a back one, so every square metre of frame carries two square metres of liquid surface.
Initial area \(= 2 \times (0.02)^2 = 2 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 8 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\)
Final area \(= 2 \times (0.03)^2 = 2 \times 9 \times 10^{-4} = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\) m\(^2\)
Increase in area:
\(dA = 2\left[(0.03)^2 - (0.02)^2\right] = 2\left(9 \times 10^{-4} - 4 \times 10^{-4}\right) = 1 \times 10^{-3}\) m\(^2\)
Work done:
\(W = T \times dA = \left(3 \times 10^{-2}\right) \times \left(1 \times 10^{-3}\right)\)
\(W = 3 \times 10^{-5}\) J
The work done in the process is **\(3 \times 10^{-5}\) J**. Forgetting the second surface would give half this value.
